definition: Hierarchical temporal memory (HTM) is a biologically constrained machine intelligence technology developed by Numenta.
details: Originally described in the 2004 book On Intelligence by Jeff Hawkins with Sandra Blakeslee, HTM is primarily used today for anomaly detection in streaming data. The technology is based on neuroscience and the physiology and interaction of pyramidal neurons in the neocortex of the mammalian (in particular, human) brain. At the core of HTM are learning algorithms that can store, learn, infer, and recall high-order sequences. Unlike most other machine learning methods, HTM constantly learns (in an unsupervised process) time-based patterns in unlabeled data. HTM is robust to noise, and has high capacity (it can learn multiple patterns simultaneously). When applied to computers, HTM is well suited for prediction, anomaly detection, classification, and ultimately sensorimotor applications. HTM has been tested and implemented in software through example applications from Numenta and a few commercial applications from Numenta's partners.

explainer.lead: Hierarchical temporal memory is a biologically constrained machine intelligence technology developed by Numenta, based on the neocortex. It is primarily used today for anomaly detection in streaming data.

tiers.eli5: It's a computer model that mimics how parts of the brain learn patterns, and it's mostly used to notice when a stream of data suddenly looks wrong.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers apply HTM to streaming anomaly detection, relying on algorithms that store, learn, infer, and recall high-order sequences. A pitfall is its contrast with most machine learning: HTM constantly learns rather than training in a separate phase.
tiers.paperLevel: HTM is a biologically constrained machine intelligence technology originally described in the 2004 book On Intelligence; at its core are learning algorithms that can store, learn, infer, and recall high-order sequences, and unlike most other machine learning methods it constantly learns.

explainer.example: A system monitoring a live data stream flags an anomaly when the incoming sequence departs from the high-order sequences the HTM has continually learned.
